what_its_for: Proparacaine is a numbing eye drop used by your eye doctor or healthcare provider to temporarily numb the surface of your eye. It is used before eye exams, eye pressure checks (tonometry), removing a foreign object from your eye, or minor eye procedures. It is NOT for use at home for eye pain.
how_to_take: This medicine is given by a healthcare professional in a clinic or doctor's office. Your provider will tilt your head back, gently pull down your lower eyelid, and place the drops directly into your eye. Keep your eye open and try not to blink right away. You may feel a brief stinging or burning sensation when the drops go in — this is normal and will pass quickly. Do NOT rub your eyes after the drops are given, as your eye will be numb and you could accidentally hurt your eye without feeling it.
dosing: Your healthcare provider will decide how many drops you need based on the procedure being performed. Usually, 1 to 2 drops are placed in the affected eye. For some longer procedures, additional drops may be given every 5 to 10 minutes as needed. You should never use this medication on your own at home.
missed_dose: This medication is given by your healthcare provider only during your visit, so there is no missed dose concern for home use. If you need to reschedule your eye procedure, contact your doctor's office to set up a new appointment.
storage: Proparacaine eye drops are stored and handled by your healthcare provider. If you are ever given a bottle to take home (which is rare and only under direct medical guidance), store it in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Keep it away from light. Do not freeze. Keep the bottle tightly closed. Throw it away if the solution changes color or becomes cloudy. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets.
what_to_avoid: Do NOT use proparacaine eye drops on your own at home to treat eye pain. Using numbing eye drops regularly can cause serious damage to the surface of your eye, including permanent vision problems. While your eye is numb, avoid rubbing, touching, or putting anything in your eye. Do not wear contact lenses until the numbness has completely worn off and your eye doctor says it is safe. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery until the numbing effect has fully worn off and your vision is back to normal.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or seek medical attention right away if you experience: increased redness or swelling of the eye after your procedure, worsening eye pain once the numbing wears off, vision changes or blurred vision that does not go away, discharge or crusting around the eye, signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, itching, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing. If you accidentally use more drops than directed or someone swallows this medication, call Poison Control right away at 1-800-222-1222.
when_it_works: Proparacaine works very quickly — your eye will usually feel numb within 30 seconds to 1 minute after the drops are applied. The numbing effect typically lasts about 10 to 20 minutes. Your healthcare provider will complete the exam or procedure during this window. Full normal sensation usually returns within 15 to 30 minutes after the drops were given.
special_populations: Tell your eye doctor before receiving proparacaine if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, as the safety in these situations is not fully established. Let your doctor know if you have any known allergies to local anesthetics (numbing medicines) such as tetracaine or benzocaine. People with certain heart conditions or those taking specific heart medications should also inform their provider. Children can receive this medication in a clinical setting, but it must always be administered by a trained healthcare professional.
